Series::acos¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::acos() const -> Series

What It Does¶

Applies the inverse cosine elementwise.

Each value is interpreted as a cosine value and mapped back to its principal angle in radians. The principal range is [0, pi], so the output is always a real angle inside that interval when the input stays inside the valid domain [-1, 1].

This is a pure elementwise transform:

  • shape is preserved

  • each element is handled independently

  • no broadcasting is involved

The important constraint is the domain. acos() is only real-valued on [-1, 1]. Values outside that interval surface as nan in the verified path shown below.

Parameters¶

None.

This is a zero-argument transform on self.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, where each element has been replaced by its principal inverse cosine in radians.

Gradient¶

Mathematically, acos(x) has derivative -1 / sqrt(1 - x^2) for interior points |x| < 1.

Two practical consequences follow from that:

  • the derivative is negative across the valid interior

  • the magnitude grows sharply as x approaches -1 or 1

On the current verified public surface used for these examples, the reverse-mode example below returns zero sensitivities rather than the mathematical derivative. So acos() should currently be treated as value-correct, but backward support is not yet reliable through this method path.

Examples¶

Example 1. Standard anchor values make the angle mapping easy to read.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0}).acos());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[3.1416, 1.5708, 1.0472, 0.0000]

Example 2. Matrices keep their shape; only the values become angles.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({
    {-1.0, -0.5},
    {0.5, 1.0},
}).acos();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[3.1415927, 2.0943951],
  [1.0471976, 0]]

Example 3. The current reverse-mode path returns zero sensitivities on this surface, which is an important present-day limitation to know.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-0.5, 0.0, 0.5});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto out = x.acos();
out.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "out=" << out << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

out=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2.0943951, 1.5707963, 1.0471976]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

Example 4. Values outside [-1, 1] are out of domain and surface as nan.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({-1.25, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.25}).acos();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[nan, 3.1415927, 1.5707963, 0, nan]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • acos() is only real-valued on [-1, 1].

  • Endpoints are valid for the forward value, but they are numerically delicate because the mathematical derivative blows up there.

  • On the current verified surface, do not assume reverse-mode support is wired just because the value transform works.

Summary¶

Use acos() when your inputs represent cosine values and you need principal angles back in radians. The two checks that matter most are domain discipline and current backward-support expectations.

See Also¶

  • Series::asin: inverse sine on the same [-1, 1] domain.

  • Series::atan: inverse tangent with no finite-domain restriction.

  • Series::cos: forward cosine transform.
